query: Controlling for priority and category, which underlying causes explain longer resolution times?

per_column.name: resolution_complexity
per_column.rationale: The nature/complexity of what must be done to resolve the ticket is a candidate underlying cause of longer resolution times -- a plausible treatment being attributed.

per_column.name: issue_severity_signal
per_column.rationale: Severity/type of issue plausibly drives both how complex/lengthy the resolution work is and the resolution time; a common cause not named in the query.

per_column.name: recurrent_issue
per_column.rationale: Whether an issue is recurrent can affect both the complexity/approach taken and the time to resolve; plausibly a common cause, surfaced from data.

per_column.name: authentication_or_access_requirement
per_column.rationale: Access/authentication involvement can shape both the resolution approach (treatment) and duration; not named in the query.

per_column.name: hardware_or_software_installation_need
per_column.rationale: Needing installation drives both the type of resolution work and the time; plausible common cause, but overlaps heavily with treatment definition.

per_column.name: scope_of_impact
per_column.rationale: Breadth of impact (company-wide vs single user) plausibly influences both the complexity of resolution effort and the duration; a genuine common cause not in the query.

per_column.name: assigned_technician
per_column.rationale: The specific technician can affect which tickets they take (assignment/complexity) and their resolution speed; a plausible common cause surfaced from data.

per_column.name: assigned_resolver_consistency
per_column.rationale: Whether the same resolver handled the ticket throughout is largely on the causal path from handling to duration; adjusting for it as a confounder is questionable.

per_column.name: closure_status_completeness
per_column.rationale: Closure completeness is an outcome/consequence of the resolution process, not a prior common cause; conditioning on it would induce bias.

per_column.name: issue_category
per_column.rationale: Category is explicitly named as something to control for in the query; a stated confounder, not a surfaced one.

judge.rationale: The added columns do set up a causal estimation: resolution_complexity acts as a candidate treatment/underlying cause of longer resolution_time, and several columns (issue_severity_signal, scope_of_impact, assigned_technician, recurrent_issue) are genuine common causes of both the resolution approach and duration that were surfaced from the data rather than copied from the query -- these demonstrate the capability under test. issue_category duplicates a control already named in the query and so does not count as a surfaced confounder. Two columns are problematic: assigned_resolver_consistency is closer to a mediator, and closure_status_completeness is a post-treatment consequence/collider whose inclusion as an adjustment variable would bias the attribution. Overall the set realises causal attribution moderately well, with several non-query confounders, but is diluted by mediator/collider inclusions and some overlap between treatment and confounder definitions.
